- All major acts, laws and policies in India relating to wildlife (Unverified) -
Name Year Purpose Details
Indian Forest Act 1927 To manage forests and protect wildlife habitats Establishes reserved and protected forests; regulates timber extraction, grazing; indirectly supports wildlife by preserving habitats; amended post-independence (1952, 1980s).
Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 1960 To prevent cruelty to animals, including wildlife Regulates treatment of animals; limited wildlife focus but sets precedent for welfare; enforced by Animal Welfare Board of India.
Import and Export (Control) Act 1947 (amended 1960s) To regulate trade in wildlife products Controls import/export of wildlife and derivatives; aligns with CITES to curb illegal trade; enforced by customs and WCCB.
Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act 1957 (amended 2015, 2020) To regulate mining to minimize environmental and wildlife impact Requires environmental clearances for mining in forest areas; ensures habitat protection; funds restoration via DMF.
Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 (amended 2002, 2006, 2022) To protect wildlife and habitats Prohibits hunting; establishes national parks, sanctuaries, conservation/community reserves; schedules (I–VI) for species protection; enforced by NTCA, WCCB.
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1974 (amended 1988) To protect aquatic ecosystems for wildlife Regulates water pollution; ensures clean rivers/lakes for species like dolphins, gharials; enforced by CPCB/SPCBs.
Forest (Conservation) Act 1980 (amended 2023) To conserve forests and wildlife habitats Restricts forest land diversion; requires central approval for non-forest use; protects biodiversity hotspots; amended to balance development.
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act 1981 (amended 1987) To protect air quality for wildlife ecosystems Regulates emissions, including noise; safeguards avian and terrestrial habitats; enforced by CPCB/SPCBs.
Environment (Protection) Act 1986 To provide an umbrella framework for environmental and wildlife protection Empowers rules for wildlife habitats (e.g., ESZs, CRZ); regulates pollution impacting biodiversity; basis for subsequent regulations.
National Forest Policy 1988 To prioritize forest conservation for wildlife Targets 33% forest cover; emphasizes ecological balance, wildlife corridors; promotes afforestation and JFM.
Biological Diversity Act 2002 (amended 2023) To conserve biological diversity and regulate resource use Establishes NBA and State Biodiversity Boards; regulates access to genetic resources; aligns with CBD, Nagoya Protocol.
Scheduled Tribes and Other Traditional Forest Dwellers (Recognition of Forest Rights) Act 2006 To recognize forest dwellers’ rights while supporting conservation Grants land and resource rights to tribal communities; promotes community-led conservation; ensures sustainable coexistence with wildlife.
National Lake Conservation Plan (NLCP) 2001 (merged 2016) To restore lakes as wildlife habitats Funds lake restoration (e.g., Dal, Chilika); merged into National Plan for Conservation of Aquatic Ecosystems; supports aquatic species.
Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification 2011 (amended 2019) To protect coastal ecosystems and marine wildlife Regulates development in CRZ-I to IV zones; protects mangroves, corals, turtle nesting sites; enforced by MoEFCC.
Island Protection Zone Notification 2011 To safeguard island biodiversity Protects Andaman & Nicobar, Lakshadweep ecosystems; regulates activities to preserve marine/terrestrial wildlife.
Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules 2010 (revised 2017) To conserve wetlands as critical wildlife habitats Prohibits harmful activities in wetlands; protects Ramsar sites (e.g., Sundarbans); supports birds, aquatic species.
National Green Tribunal (NGT) Act 2010 To adjudicate environmental and wildlife disputes Establishes NGT; enforces wildlife laws (e.g., WPA, EPA); applies polluter-pays principle; fast-tracks cases.
Green Highways (Plantation, Transplantation, Beautification & Maintenance) Policy 2015 To enhance wildlife corridors via afforestation Mandates plantation along highways; supports habitat connectivity, carbon sequestration; managed by NHAI.
Nagoya Protocol (Adoption) 2014 To ensure fair sharing of genetic resources Implements CBD’s access and benefit-sharing; protects wildlife genetic resources; enforced via Biological Diversity Act.
- All legal bodies, organizations, of India related to wildlife (Unverified) -
Name Establishment Year Purpose Details
Animal Welfare Board of India (AWBI) 1962 To promote animal welfare and prevent cruelty Statutory body under Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960; advises on wildlife welfare, regulates captive animals, and supports anti-cruelty enforcement; headquartered in Chennai.
Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) 1883 To conduct research and advocacy for wildlife conservation Non-governmental organization; conducts biodiversity research (e.g., bird ringing, vulture conservation); influences policy; key projects include IBAs and Sundarbans studies.
Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) 1974 To regulate pollution impacting wildlife habitats Statutory body under Water Act, 1974; monitors water/air quality; protects aquatic ecosystems (e.g., rivers for dolphins); coordinates with SPCBs.
Central Zoo Authority (CZA) 1992 To regulate zoos and captive breeding Statutory body under Wildlife Protection Act, 1972; oversees zoo standards, endangered species breeding (e.g., red panda); ensures ethical treatment; 150+ recognized zoos.
Compensatory Afforestation Fund Management and Planning Authority (CAMPA) 2009 (formalized 2016) To manage funds for afforestation and habitat restoration Statutory body under Forest Conservation Act; uses funds from forest land diversion (~Rs. 66,000 Cr by 2025) for afforestation, wildlife corridor restoration.
Joint Forest Management (JFM) 1990 To involve communities in forest and wildlife conservation Policy framework under National Forest Policy, 1988; partners local communities with forest departments; protects habitats via sustainable management; 100,000+ committees.
Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) 1985 (as MoEF, renamed 2014) To oversee environmental and wildlife policies Central ministry; formulates/enforces wildlife laws (e.g., WPA, EPA); manages protected areas, projects (Tiger, Elephant); coordinates with NBA, NTCA; HQ in New Delhi.
Ministry of Tribal Affairs 1999 To support tribal communities in wildlife areas Implements Forest Rights Act, 2006; ensures tribal rights in forests; balances conservation with livelihoods; supports community-led wildlife protection.
National Afforestation and Eco-Development Board (NAEB) 1992 To promote afforestation for wildlife habitats MoEFCC body; funds afforestation, eco-restoration; supports biodiversity via National Afforestation Programme; enhances forest cover for wildlife.
National Biodiversity Authority (NBA) 2003 To conserve biodiversity and regulate resource use Statutory body under Biological Diversity Act, 2002; implements CBD, Nagoya Protocol; regulates access to genetic resources; supports State Biodiversity Boards.
National Ganga River Basin Authority (NGRBA) 2009 To protect Ganges ecosystem and aquatic wildlife MoEFCC-led; restores Ganges water quality; conserves species like Ganges River Dolphin; merged into National Mission for Clean Ganga (2016) but retains wildlife focus.
National Green Tribunal (NGT) 2010 To adjudicate environmental and wildlife disputes Statutory body under NGT Act, 2010; enforces wildlife laws (e.g., WPA, EPA); applies polluter-pays principle; benches across India; fast-tracks cases.
National Tiger Conservation Authority (NTCA) 2005 To oversee tiger conservation Statutory body under Wildlife Protection Act, 1972; manages Project Tiger (58 reserves, ~75,000 km² by 2025); anti-poaching, habitat restoration.
Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB) 2006 To combat illegal wildlife trade Statutory body under Wildlife Protection Act, 1972; coordinates enforcement; aligns with CITES; operates 5 regional offices; combats poaching, trafficking.
Wildlife Institute of India (WII) 1982 To conduct wildlife research and training Autonomous MoEFCC institute; trains forest officers; researches endangered species (e.g., tigers, snow leopards); supports policy formulation; based in Dehradun.
Wildlife Trust of India (WTI) 1998 To support wildlife rescue and conservation NGO; focuses on species rehabilitation (e.g., rhinos, elephants); anti-poaching advocacy; partners with MoEFCC; operates in Assam, Arunachal, etc.
- All legal bodies, organizations, etc of the world for wildlife, climate like SITES, etc, their establishment, and purpose, some of them I know I will include (Unverified) -
Name Establishment Year Purpose Details
International Whaling Commission (IWC) 1946 To regulate whaling and conserve whale populations Established under the International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling; 88 member countries; enforces 1986 commercial whaling moratorium; addresses climate impacts on marine mammals through scientific research and habitat protection; UPSC relevance: Links to ocean conservation under SDG 14; secretariat in Cambridge, UK.
International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) 1948 To promote nature conservation and sustainable use of resources Global authority with 1,400+ members (states, NGOs); publishes Red List of Threatened Species (160,000+ species assessed); hosts World Conservation Congress; integrates climate adaptation and biodiversity; UPSC relevance: Key for endangered species questions; HQ in Gland, Switzerland.
Ramsar Convention on Wetlands 1971 To promote conservation and wise use of wetlands Intergovernmental treaty with 172 parties; designates 2,500+ Ramsar sites (260M hectares); supports climate resilience via wetland carbon sinks and flood mitigation; UPSC relevance: India's 82 sites (e.g., Sundarbans) often in PYQs; secretariat in Gland, Switzerland.
Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) 1973 To regulate international trade in endangered species UN treaty with 184 parties; protects 38,000+ species via three appendices; enforces trade controls to prevent poaching; aligns with climate goals by preserving habitats; UPSC relevance: Schedules for species protection, links to WPA 1972; secretariat in Geneva.
The Wildlife Trade Monitoring Network (TRAFFIC) 1976 To monitor and combat illegal wildlife trade Joint IUCN/WWF program; operates in 50+ countries; analyzes trade data, supports CITES enforcement; addresses climate-driven poaching pressures; UPSC relevance: Wildlife crime trends in current affairs; HQ in Cambridge, UK.
Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species (CMS) 1979 To conserve migratory species and their habitats UN treaty with 133 parties; protects terrestrial, aquatic, avian migrants; initiatives like Central Asian Flyway; addresses climate impacts on migration routes; UPSC relevance: India's flyway importance (e.g., Amur falcons); secretariat in Bonn, Germany.
World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) 1961 To conserve wildlife and reduce human impact on ecosystems Global NGO; works in 100+ countries; leads projects like Tx2 (tiger doubling), Earth Hour; funds climate adaptation, forest restoration; UPSC relevance: NGO roles in conservation; HQ in Gland, Switzerland.
Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer 1985 To protect the ozone layer through international cooperation UN framework treaty with 198 parties; led to Montreal Protocol; protects ecosystems from UV radiation, indirectly aiding climate goals; UPSC relevance: Ozone depletion vs. climate change distinction; secretariat in Nairobi.
International Tropical Timber Organization (ITTO) 1986 To promote sustainable tropical forest management and trade Intergovernmental body under ITTA 2006; 71 members; funds 1,300+ projects for SFM, biodiversity; supports climate mitigation via forests; UPSC relevance: Forest cover and REDD+ linkages; HQ in Yokohama, Japan.
Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer 1987 To phase out ozone-depleting substances UN treaty with 198 parties; Kigali Amendment (2016) phases down HFCs, avoiding 0.5°C warming by 2100; protects climate-sensitive ecosystems; UPSC relevance: Success story in MEAs; secretariat in Nairobi.
United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (UNCED) 1992 To establish a global agenda for sustainable development Rio Earth Summit; produced Rio Declaration, Agenda 21, CBD, UNFCCC; foundational for climate and biodiversity frameworks; UPSC relevance: SDGs precursor; one-time event with lasting impact.
United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) 1992 To stabilize greenhouse gas concentrations UN treaty with 198 parties; oversees COPs (e.g., Kyoto, Paris Agreement); facilitates NDCs, climate finance ($100B+ annually); UPSC relevance: Core of IR-environment questions; secretariat in Bonn, Germany.
Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) 1992 To conserve biodiversity, promote sustainable use, and ensure benefit-sharing UN treaty with 196 parties; Kunming-Montreal Framework (2022) sets 30x30 goal (30% land/ocean protected by 2030); links biodiversity to climate; UPSC relevance: Nagoya Protocol, Aichi Targets; secretariat in Montreal.
Global Environment Facility (GEF) 1992 To fund environmental projects in developing countries Financial mechanism for CBD, UNFCCC, UNCCD; $22B+ for 5,000+ projects; supports biodiversity, climate mitigation/adaptation; UPSC relevance: Funding for Global South; secretariat in Washington, D.C.
BirdLife International 1993 To conserve birds and their habitats Global partnership of 120+ NGOs; manages IBAs (13,000+ sites); Red List authority for birds; supports climate adaptation for avian species; UPSC relevance: Migratory birds under CMS; HQ in Cambridge, UK.
Global Tiger Forum (GTF) 1993 To promote global tiger conservation Intergovernmental body with 13 tiger-range countries; supports Tx2 goal (double tigers by 2022); anti-poaching, habitat restoration; UPSC relevance: Project Tiger links; HQ in New Delhi, India.
United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) 1994 To combat desertification and promote land resilience UN treaty with 197 parties; Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) framework; enhances climate resilience in drylands; UPSC relevance: Desertification in arid India; secretariat in Bonn, Germany.
Invasive Species Specialist Group (ISSG) 1994 To reduce threats from invasive alien species IUCN SSC group; manages Global Invasive Species Database; advises on climate-driven invasive risks; UPSC relevance: IAS threats to biodiversity; based in Auckland, New Zealand.
Rotterdam Convention 1998 To regulate international trade of hazardous chemicals UN treaty with 166 parties; prior informed consent for 50+ chemicals; protects ecosystems from toxics, aiding climate resilience; UPSC relevance: Chemical pollution links to health/environment; secretariat in Geneva/Rome.
United Nations Forum on Forests (UNFF) 2000 To promote sustainable forest management UN body with 197 members; Non-Legally Binding Instrument on Forests (2007); supports REDD+, climate mitigation; UPSC relevance: Forest policy questions; secretariat in New York.
Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) 2001 To eliminate or restrict POPs UN treaty with 186 parties; targets 30+ chemicals; reduces environmental toxins impacting climate-sensitive ecosystems; UPSC relevance: Persistent pollutants in GS3; secretariat in Geneva.
Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (MA) 2001 To assess ecosystem changes and human well-being UN-led assessment (2001–2005); informed CBD, MDGs; highlighted ecosystem-climate links; UPSC relevance: Ecosystem services in ecology; one-time project with global policy impact.
Coalition Against Wildlife Trafficking (CAWT) 2005 To combat illegal wildlife trafficking US-led voluntary coalition (6 governments, 13 NGOs); strengthens enforcement, reduces demand; focuses on tigers, rhinos; UPSC relevance: Transnational crime in IR; coordinates with CITES.
Global Climate Change Alliance (GCCA) 2007 To support climate action in developing countries EU initiative for LDCs/SIDS; €10B+ funding; integrates climate into development; supports adaptation, mitigation in 80+ countries; UPSC relevance: EU-India climate partnerships.
The Climate Group 2004 To drive climate action by businesses and governments Nonprofit with 500+ corporate/government partners; runs EV100, RE100; Under2 Coalition for subnational net-zero; UPSC relevance: Non-state actors in climate governance; HQ in London.
International Energy Agency (IEA) 1974 To ensure energy security and promote sustainable energy Intergovernmental organization with 31 members; advises on clean energy transitions; Net Zero by 2050 roadmap; tracks climate policies; UPSC relevance: Energy security in GS3; HQ in Paris.
Global Plastic Treaty (INC Process) 2022 To end plastic pollution through a legally binding treaty UNEA resolution (UNEP/EA.5/Res.14); negotiations via Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC-1 to INC-5); targets full lifecycle plastic management; UPSC relevance: Emerging MEA for SDG 14/12; expected finalization 2024, entry 2025.
Global Methane Pledge 2021 To reduce global methane emissions by 30% by 2030 Launched at COP26; 150+ countries; focuses on fossil fuels, agriculture, waste; short-term climate impact (SLCPs); UPSC relevance: Ties to Paris Agreement, India's methane targets.
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) 2022 To halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030 CBD COP15 outcome; 4 goals, 23 targets (e.g., 30x30 protection); $200B annual funding; UPSC relevance: Successor to Aichi Targets, links to SDG 15; secretariat in Montreal.
High Seas Treaty (BBNJ Agreement) 2023 To conserve marine biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction UNCLOS implementation; protects 30% oceans by 2030; environmental impact assessments; UPSC relevance: Ocean governance, India's EEZ extension; 90+ signatories, ratification ongoing.
Loss and Damage Fund 2022 (operationalized 2023) To provide financial support for climate-vulnerable countries COP27 establishment; $700M+ initial pledges; operational at COP28; UPSC relevance: Equity in climate finance, Global South demands; hosted by World Bank.
System for the Integrated Assessment and Modelling of Global Climate and Biodiversity Impacts (SITES) 2018 To model climate and biodiversity impacts Swedish research infrastructure; supports IPCC, CBD with scenario-based assessments; aids policy for climate-biodiversity nexus; UPSC relevance: Scientific tools for IR; based in Stockholm.
UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration (2021–2030) 2021 To prevent, halt, and reverse ecosystem degradation UN initiative (UNEP, FAO); focuses on restoration for climate resilience, biodiversity; UPSC relevance: Links to UNCCD, CBD; involves 100+ countries/projects.
Coalition for Sovereign Debt Conversions for Climate and Conservation 2024 To scale funding for climate and nature via debt-for-nature swaps Led by 6 NGOs (WWF, Conservation International, etc.); unlocks $100B+ potential; UPSC relevance: Innovative finance for SDGs, debt relief in Global South; announced at COP29.
COP28 UAE Consensus 2023 To accelerate global climate action post-global stocktake COP28 outcome; transitions from fossil fuels; triples renewables by 2030; UPSC relevance: First explicit fossil fuel phase-out mention; operationalizes loss/damage.
- All Indian initiatives on climate change (Unverified) -
Name Establishment Year Purpose Details
Precursors to Climate Policy
Environment (Protection) Act 1986 To provide a legal framework for environmental protection, including pollution control Enacted post-Bhopal disaster, this act empowers the central government to regulate emissions, waste, and industrial activities. It established standards for air, water, and soil quality, indirectly supporting climate goals by reducing pollutants like black carbon. Achievements: Enabled 1,500+ environmental regulations, including vehicle emission norms (BS-VI). Challenges: Weak enforcement and judicial delays. It laid the groundwork for climate-focused policies like NAPCC. Administered by MoEFCC.
National Forest Policy 1988 To enhance forest cover and promote ecological balance Targets 33% forest cover (current: 24.6%, ISFR 2021); promotes afforestation, Joint Forest Management (JFM), and biodiversity conservation. It supports carbon sequestration (2.5 Gt CO2e stored in Indian forests). Achievements: 10M hectares afforested since 1988. Challenges: Land conflicts, urban encroachment. It influenced NAPCC’s Green India Mission and aligns with SDG 15. Administered by MoEFCC.
Energy Conservation Act 2001 To promote energy efficiency and reduce energy intensity Established the Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE); mandates efficiency standards for appliances (Star Labeling) and industries. Achievements: Reduced energy intensity by 20% (2001–2020), saving 300 Mt CO2e. Challenges: Limited MSME adoption, high retrofit costs. It laid the foundation for NMEEE and PAT, aligning with India’s early mitigation efforts. Administered by Ministry of Power.
National Environment Policy (NEP) 2006 To integrate environmental concerns into development planning Outlines principles for sustainable development, emphasizing climate adaptation (e.g., disaster resilience) and mitigation (e.g., clean energy). Achievements: Guided NAPCC formulation and green accounting (e.g., TEEB adoption). Challenges: Limited mainstreaming across sectors. It set the stage for India’s climate policy framework, influencing state action plans. Administered by MoEFCC.
Core Climate Change Initiatives
National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) 2008 To outline India’s strategy for climate change mitigation and adaptation Launched by PM’s Council, NAPCC comprises 8 missions addressing solar, energy efficiency, agriculture, water, forests, urban habitats, Himalayas, and knowledge. Updated in 2021 with Panchamrit pledges (500 GW non-fossil by 2030, net-zero by 2070). Achievements: 175 GW renewables by 2025, 2.8 Gt CO2e sequestered via forests. Challenges: Funding gaps (Rs. 10L Cr needed) and inter-ministerial coordination. It drives India’s NDCs and global commitments. Administered by MoEFCC.
R2 Code of Practices 2008 (adopted in India) To ensure responsible recycling of electronic waste Adopted under SERI’s Responsible Recycling (R2) standard, it promotes safe e-waste management, data security, and environmental sustainability. Achievements: 200+ certified recyclers in India, processing 1.2M tonnes e-waste annually (2024). Challenges: Informal sector dominance (90% of e-waste), lack of awareness. It reduces GHG emissions from improper disposal, aligning with circular economy goals. Administered by CPCB.
Common Carbon Metric (CCM) 2010 (adopted in India) To standardize carbon footprint assessment for buildings UNEP-supported tool under Sustainable Habitat Mission; measures GHG emissions from construction and operations. Achievements: Adopted in 500+ green building projects (e.g., IGBC-rated), saving 10 Mt CO2e annually. Challenges: High implementation costs, limited uptake in smaller cities. It supports urban decarbonization and aligns with SDG 11. Administered by BEE and MoEFCC.
National Solar Mission (NSM) 2010 To promote solar energy for emissions reduction and energy security Part of NAPCC; targets 100 GW solar by 2022 (81 GW achieved by 2025). Includes rooftop solar (15 GW), solar parks (40 GW), and off-grid systems. Achievements: Reduced 200 Mt CO2e, powered 20M households. Challenges: Land acquisition, grid integration. It drives India’s 50% non-fossil NDC target. Administered by MNRE.
National Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (NMEEE) 2010 To improve energy efficiency across industries and buildings Part of NAPCC; includes PAT scheme, ESCerts trading, and appliance standards. Achievements: Saved 20M tonnes oil equivalent, 80 Mt CO2e (2012–2025). Challenges: High upfront costs, MSME compliance gaps. It reduced India’s energy intensity by 25% (2010–2020), supporting NDCs. Administered by BEE, Ministry of Power.
National Mission on Sustainable Habitat 2010 To promote sustainability in urban planning and infrastructure Part of NAPCC; focuses on green buildings, urban transport (e.g., metro expansion), and waste management. Integrates CCM for emissions tracking. Achievements: 7,000+ green buildings, 1,200 km metro lines by 2025. Challenges: Urban sprawl, funding shortages. It aligns with SDG 11 and Smart Cities Mission. Administered by MoHUA.
National Water Mission 2010 To ensure water security under climate change impacts Part of NAPCC; promotes water efficiency, basin management, and groundwater recharge. Achievements: 10,000+ water conservation projects, 20% improved irrigation efficiency. Challenges: Inter-state water disputes, over-extraction. It addresses climate-induced water scarcity, supporting SDG 6. Administered by Jal Shakti Ministry.
National Mission for Sustaining Himalayan Ecosystem 2010 To protect Himalayan ecosystems from climate impacts Part of NAPCC; focuses on glacier monitoring, biodiversity, and livelihoods. Achievements: Established 5 research centers, mapped 40% of Himalayan glaciers. Challenges: Data gaps, cross-border coordination. It addresses melting glaciers (1.5M km² ice loss) and aligns with SDG 15. Administered by MoEFCC.
Perform, Achieve, and Trade (PAT) Scheme 2012 To enhance energy efficiency in energy-intensive industries Under NMEEE; targets sectors like steel, cement, thermal power. Achievements: Saved 20M tonnes oil equivalent, traded 15M ESCerts (2024). Challenges: Limited MSME inclusion, high monitoring costs. It reduced 100 Mt CO2e emissions, supporting India’s NDCs. Administered by BEE.
National Mission for a Green India (GIM) 2014 To increase forest cover for carbon sequestration and biodiversity Part of NAPCC; targets 5M hectares afforestation, 6M hectares ecosystem restoration. Achievements: Afforested 2M hectares, sequestered 100 Mt CO2e by 2025. Challenges: Land availability, community conflicts. It aligns with SDG 15 and India’s 2.5–3 Gt CO2e sink NDC. Administered by MoEFCC.
National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA) 2014 To enhance agricultural resilience to climate variability Part of NAPCC; promotes climate-resilient crops, water-efficient irrigation (e.g., drip), and soil health cards. Achievements: 10M farmers adopted practices, 15% yield increase in rainfed areas. Challenges: Farmer awareness, input costs. Includes CSV pilots. Aligns with SDG 2. Administered by Ministry of Agriculture.
Climate-Smart Villages (CSV) 2015 To pilot climate-resilient agricultural practices in vulnerable regions CGIAR/CCAFS initiative under NMSA; implemented in 150+ villages (Haryana, Bihar, Andhra Pradesh). Practices include laser land leveling, alternate wetting-drying, and drought-resistant seeds. Achievements: 30% water savings, 20% yield increase in pilots. Challenges: Scaling to 600,000 villages, funding. It enhances farmer resilience to climate shocks. Administered by ICAR.
International Solar Alliance (ISA) 2015 To promote solar energy globally through cooperation India-France initiative with 121 members; targets $1T solar investment by 2030. Achievements: Facilitated 10,000 MW solar projects, trained 50,000 technicians. Challenges: Financing gaps, technology access. It positions India as a renewable energy leader, supporting global NDCs. Secretariat in Gurugram.
National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC) 2015 To finance adaptation projects in climate-vulnerable sectors Rs. 1,000 Cr corpus; funds 30+ projects in agriculture, water, and coastal areas (e.g., Odisha’s mangrove restoration). Achievements: Benefited 1M farmers, restored 50,000 hectares. Challenges: Limited scale, bureaucratic delays. It supports community-based adaptation, aligning with SDG 13. Administered by MoEFCC.
Faster Adoption and Manufacturing of Electric Vehicles (FAME-I) 2015 To promote electric vehicle adoption for transport decarbonization Rs. 795 Cr scheme; subsidized 1.4 lakh EVs (mostly 2/3-wheelers). Achievements: Reduced 2 Mt CO2e, spurred EV manufacturing. Challenges: Limited charging infrastructure, high costs. It laid the foundation for FAME-II and India’s EV push. Administered by Ministry of Heavy Industries.
National Mission for Clean Ganga (NMCG) 2015 To rejuvenate the Ganga river basin for ecosystem restoration Under Namami Gange (Rs. 37,000 Cr); builds STPs, restores biodiversity (e.g., Gangetic dolphins). Achievements: 4,000+ villages ODF, 2,500 km river cleaned. Challenges: Industrial pollution, funding utilization. It enhances climate resilience via river ecosystems, aligning with SDG 6. Administered by Jal Shakti Ministry.
PM-KUSUM 2018 To solarize agriculture for farmer income and emissions reduction Targets 30 GW solar pumps and decentralized plants (10,000 MW achieved by 2025). Achievements: 2M solar pumps installed, 15 Mt CO2e reduced. Challenges: High upfront costs, grid connectivity. It supports rural livelihoods and NDC renewable goals. Administered by MNRE.
National Mission on Bamboo 2018 (restructured) To promote bamboo as a climate-resilient resource Promotes bamboo plantations, processing, and livelihoods across 10 states. Achievements: 1M hectares planted, 5 Mt CO2e sequestered annually. Challenges: Market development, farmer adoption. It supports agroforestry and SDG 15. Administered by Ministry of Agriculture.
National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) 2019 To reduce air pollution in urban areas with climate co-benefits Targets 20–30% PM2.5/PM10 reduction in 131 cities by 2026 (Rs. 9,600 Cr). Achievements: 40% PM reduction in 20 cities, 50 Mt CO2e co-benefits. Challenges: Vehicular emissions, stubble burning. It aligns with SDG 11 and climate mitigation. Administered by MoEFCC.
FAME-II 2019 To accelerate EV adoption and charging infrastructure Rs. 10,000 Cr scheme; supports 1.5M EVs, 8,000 charging stations by 2025. Achievements: 10% EV penetration in 2-wheelers, 20 Mt CO2e reduced. Challenges: Battery costs, rural charging gaps. It supports India’s NDC transport goals. Administered by Ministry of Heavy Industries.
One Sun One World One Grid (OSOWOG) 2019 To create a global renewable energy grid for solar power sharing India-UK initiative; aims to interconnect 140 countries for 3,000 GW solar by 2030. Achievements: Pilot projects in South Asia (e.g., India-Sri Lanka). Challenges: Geopolitical coordination, infrastructure costs. It enhances global renewable access, aligning with ISA. Secretariat in Gurugram.
National Hydrogen Mission 2021 To develop green hydrogen as a clean fuel for hard-to-abate sectors Targets 5M tonnes green hydrogen by 2030, 5 GW electrolyser capacity. Achievements: 10 pilot projects, 1 GW electrolyser tenders. Challenges: High production costs (Rs. 300/kg), infrastructure gaps. It supports India’s net-zero pathway. Administered by MNRE.
Lifestyle for Environment (LiFE) 2022 To promote sustainable lifestyles globally India-led at COP26; promotes mindful consumption (e.g., energy, water saving). Achievements: Adopted by 100+ countries, 10M Indian households engaged. Challenges: Behavioral change scalability. It enhances India’s climate diplomacy, aligning with SDG 12. Administered by MoEFCC.
Green Credit Programme 2023 To incentivize voluntary environmental actions Under Green Credit Rules; rewards tree plantation, water conservation with tradeable credits. Achievements: 500 projects registered, 10,000 hectares restored. Challenges: Market development, verification systems. It supports mitigation/adaptation, aligning with SDG 13. Administered by MoEFCC.
National Green Hydrogen Mission 2023 To establish India as a global green hydrogen hub Rs. 19,744 Cr; targets 5 GW electrolyser capacity, 10% export share by 2030. Achievements: 20 pilot plants, Rs. 3,000 Cr incentives disbursed. Challenges: Technology maturity, high costs. It drives decarbonization in industry, transport. Administered by MNRE.
PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana 2024 To install rooftop solar in 100M households Rs. 75,000 Cr scheme; provides free 300 units/month electricity. Achievements: 5M households covered, 2 GW installed (2025). Challenges: Supply chain constraints, awareness gaps. It supports energy access and NDC renewable targets. Administered by MNRE.
PM E-DRIVE Scheme 2025 To boost EV adoption and charging infrastructure Rs. 4,000 Cr for 2025–2027; targets 2M 2-wheelers, 24,000 buses. Achievements: Launched with 10,000 chargers planned. Challenges: Battery supply, rural adoption. It reduces transport emissions, aligning with NDCs and Budget 2025. Administered by Ministry of Heavy Industries.
- All global initiatives on climate change (Unverified) -
Name Establishment Year Purpose Details
Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer 1985 To establish a framework for international cooperation to protect the ozone layer Adopted in Vienna with 198 parties, this UN treaty provides the foundational framework for the Montreal Protocol. It promotes research, monitoring, and data exchange on ozone depletion, focusing on protecting ecosystems from harmful UV radiation. Achievements include global cooperation on ozone science, enabling subsequent binding commitments. Challenges include ensuring compliance in developing nations with limited monitoring capacity. It indirectly supports climate goals by protecting ecosystems vulnerable to climate change. Secretariat in Nairobi.
Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer 1987 To phase out production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances Adopted under the Vienna Convention, this UN treaty (198 parties) targets substances like CFCs and halons. The 2016 Kigali Amendment phases down HFCs, potent GHGs, projected to avoid 0.5°C warming by 2100. It has phased out 98% of ozone-depleting substances since 1987, restoring the ozone layer significantly. Mechanisms include the Multilateral Fund ($4.4B since 1991) for developing countries. Challenges include illegal CFC trade and HFC phase-down costs. It supports climate-sensitive ecosystems like coral reefs. Secretariat in Nairobi.
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) 1988 To provide scientific assessments on climate change causes, impacts, and solutions Established by UNEP/WMO, with 195 members, the IPCC produces comprehensive reports (e.g., AR6, 2021–2023) synthesizing global climate science. It details warming trajectories (1.1°C by 2020, 1.5°C risk by 2030s), impacts (e.g., sea-level rise, extreme weather), and mitigation/adaptation strategies. Its reports guide UNFCCC negotiations and national policies. Challenges include translating complex science into policy action and addressing political resistance. The IPCC has shaped global climate discourse, earning a Nobel Peace Prize in 2007. Secretariat in Geneva.
Basel Convention 1989 To regulate transboundary movements of hazardous wastes and ensure their environmentally sound management Adopted with 191 parties, this UN treaty controls hazardous waste trade, preventing dumping in developing nations. It covers e-waste, plastics, and chemicals, reducing environmental pollution that exacerbates climate impacts. Mechanisms include prior informed consent and technical guidelines. Achievements include a 2019 plastic waste amendment to curb marine pollution. Challenges involve enforcement gaps and illegal waste trafficking. It supports climate goals by reducing ecosystem degradation. Secretariat in Geneva.
United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) 1992 To stabilize greenhouse gas concentrations to prevent dangerous climate interference Adopted at Rio Summit with 198 parties, the UNFCCC is the primary global climate treaty. It hosts annual COPs, leading to Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement, and mechanisms like CDM and REDD+. It facilitates climate finance ($100B/year goal), technology transfer, and NDCs. Achievements include near-universal participation and Paris Agreement adoption. Challenges include slow progress on finance and ambition gaps (2.4–3.5°C warming trajectory). It shapes global climate governance. Secretariat in Bonn, Germany.
Agenda 21 1992 To provide a comprehensive action plan for sustainable development Adopted at Rio Summit, this non-binding UN plan outlines sustainable development strategies across economic, social, and environmental domains. It emphasizes climate action through energy efficiency, forest conservation, and technology transfer. It led to frameworks like UNFCCC and SDGs. Achievements include mainstreaming sustainability in national policies. Challenges include voluntary nature and uneven implementation. It influenced India’s NAPCC and global green policies. Secretariat in New York.
Global Environment Facility (GEF) 1992 To provide financial support for environmental projects in developing countries Established as a financial mechanism for UNFCCC, CBD, and UNCCD, the GEF has disbursed $22B+ for 5,000+ projects across 170+ countries. It funds mitigation (e.g., renewables), adaptation (e.g., coastal resilience), and biodiversity. Mechanisms include grants, loans, and co-financing. Achievements include supporting 40% of global protected areas. Challenges include limited funding relative to needs ($1T/year gap). It’s critical for Global South climate action. Secretariat in Washington, D.C.
United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) 1994 To combat desertification, land degradation, and drought in drylands Adopted at Rio Summit with 197 parties, the UNCCD promotes sustainable land management through the Land Degradation Neutrality (LDN) framework. It addresses climate-driven land degradation, supporting resilience in agriculture and ecosystems. Achievements include LDN adoption in 130+ countries, restoring 450M hectares. Challenges include funding shortages and slow implementation. It aligns with SDG 15 and supports climate adaptation. Secretariat in Bonn, Germany.
National Greenhouse Gas Inventories Programme (NGGIP) 1995 To develop standardized methodologies for GHG emissions inventories An IPCC program supporting UNFCCC, it provides guidelines for countries to measure and report GHG emissions (e.g., CO2, methane). It ensures transparency and consistency in NDC reporting. Achievements include global adoption of 2006 IPCC Guidelines, updated in 2019 for accuracy. Challenges include data gaps in developing nations and capacity constraints. It’s critical for tracking Paris Agreement progress. Secretariat hosted by IPCC in Geneva.
Kyoto Protocol (COP3) 1997 To set binding GHG emission reduction targets for developed countries Adopted at COP3 in Kyoto with 192 parties, it mandated 5% GHG cuts below 1990 levels (2008–2012) for Annex I countries. Mechanisms included Clean Development Mechanism (CDM, 7,800 projects), emissions trading, and Joint Implementation. Achievements: Reduced emissions by 2.4 Gt CO2e in first period. Challenges: Non-participation of USA, limited second commitment (2013–2020). It paved the way for Paris Agreement. Secretariat in Bonn.
Greenhouse Gas Protocol 1998 To provide standardized tools for corporate and organizational GHG accounting Developed by WRI and WBCSD, this protocol offers frameworks (e.g., Corporate Standard, Scope 3) for measuring emissions across value chains. Adopted by 90% of Fortune 500 companies, it supports NDC alignment and net-zero targets. Achievements include enabling 10,000+ organizations to report emissions. Challenges include data accuracy and Scope 3 complexity. It drives corporate climate action globally. Secretariat in Washington, D.C.
Rotterdam Convention 1998 To promote shared responsibility in the international trade of hazardous chemicals UN treaty with 166 parties; requires prior informed consent for 50+ chemicals (e.g., pesticides, industrial chemicals). It protects ecosystems from toxic pollution, supporting climate resilience. Achievements include regulating 1.2M tonnes of chemical trade annually. Challenges include enforcement in low-capacity countries and industry resistance. It complements Stockholm Convention. Secretariat in Geneva/Rome.
International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture (ITPGRFA) 2001 To ensure access to plant genetic resources for food security and climate resilience FAO treaty with 149 parties; facilitates access to 64 crops via a multilateral system, supporting climate-resilient agriculture. Achievements include 5.7M seed samples shared globally, aiding drought-resistant varieties. Challenges include benefit-sharing disputes and funding for genebanks. It aligns with SDG 2 and CBD’s Nagoya Protocol. Secretariat in Rome.
Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants (POPs) 2001 To eliminate or restrict persistent organic pollutants UN treaty with 186 parties; targets 30+ POPs (e.g., DDT, PCBs) that harm ecosystems and health. Mechanisms include national implementation plans and financial assistance. Achievements: Reduced 80% of targeted POPs globally. Challenges: Emerging POPs and disposal costs. It supports climate goals by reducing toxins in vulnerable ecosystems. Secretariat in Geneva.
Bali Action Plan (COP13) 2007 To advance long-term cooperative climate action Adopted at COP13 in Bali, this UNFCCC roadmap outlined four pillars: mitigation, adaptation, finance, and technology. It launched REDD and negotiations for a post-Kyoto framework. Achievements include mobilizing $30B in fast-start finance (2010–2012). Challenges: Lack of binding commitments slowed progress. It set the stage for Copenhagen and Paris agreements. Secretariat in Bonn.
REDD & REDD+ (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation) 2007 To incentivize forest conservation to reduce GHG emissions Introduced at COP13, REDD+ (adopted 2013 via Warsaw Framework) includes conservation and sustainable forest management. It incentivizes developing countries with payments for verified carbon storage (e.g., $5B disbursed). Achievements: 50+ countries with REDD+ programs, saving 6 Gt CO2e. Challenges: Land tenure disputes, monitoring accuracy. It aligns with SDG 15 and UNFCCC. Secretariat in Bonn.
Earth Hour 2007 To raise global awareness about climate change through symbolic action WWF-led campaign; annual one-hour lights-off event in 190+ countries, engaging 2.2B people. It promotes energy conservation and climate action. Achievements include influencing local policies (e.g., renewable energy adoption in cities). Challenges: Limited measurable impact beyond awareness. It fosters public engagement in climate solutions. Secretariat in Gland, Switzerland.
The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity (TEEB) 2007 To integrate economic value of ecosystems into decision-making UNEP-led initiative; quantifies ecosystem services (e.g., $125T/year globally). It informs UNFCCC, CBD, and national policies (e.g., India’s Green Accounting). Achievements: Adopted by 60+ countries for policy integration. Challenges: Valuation complexity and policy uptake. It highlights climate-biodiversity linkages. Secretariat in Geneva.
Forest Carbon Partnership Facility (FCPF) 2008 To build capacity for REDD+ in developing countries World Bank initiative with $1.1B for 47 countries; supports readiness (e.g., national strategies) and results-based payments for carbon credits. Achievements: 15 countries with verified emissions reductions. Challenges: Slow disbursement, governance issues. It supports forest-based climate mitigation. Secretariat in Washington, D.C.
Climate Action Tracker 2009 To independently assess climate pledges and progress Run by Climate Analytics and NewClimate Institute; evaluates NDCs of 40+ countries, projecting 2.4–3.5°C warming based on current policies. It critiques ambition gaps (e.g., India’s strong renewables vs. coal reliance). Achievements: Influences policy debates and COP negotiations. Challenges: Limited enforcement power. It enhances transparency in global climate action. Secretariat in Berlin.
Copenhagen Accord (COP15) 2009 To establish voluntary climate commitments Adopted at COP15 in Copenhagen, this non-binding UNFCCC agreement set a 2°C warming limit and pledged $100B/year climate finance by 2020 for developing countries. It introduced INDCs. Achievements: 141 countries submitted pledges. Challenges: Lack of binding targets and finance delays. It bridged Kyoto to Paris Agreement. Secretariat in Bonn.
Cancun Agreements (COP16) 2010 To formalize climate commitments and establish mechanisms Adopted at COP16 in Cancun, it formalized Copenhagen pledges, established the Green Climate Fund ($10.3B by 2020), and set up technology and adaptation frameworks. Achievements: Advanced REDD+ and loss/damage discussions. Challenges: Slow GCF operationalization. It strengthened UNFCCC processes. Secretariat in Bonn.
Minamata Convention on Mercury 2013 To protect human health and ecosystems from mercury emissions UN treaty with 147 parties; regulates mercury use in mining, industry, and products. Achievements: Reduced global mercury emissions by 20% since 2013. Challenges: Artisanal mining and compliance costs. It supports climate resilience by reducing ecosystem toxins. Secretariat in Geneva.
BioCarbon Fund Initiative for Sustainable Forest Landscapes 2013 To promote low-carbon land use through sustainable forestry World Bank program with $350M; supports REDD+ in 6 countries (e.g., Colombia, Ethiopia). It integrates agriculture, forestry, and livelihoods. Achievements: Reduced 50 Mt CO2e emissions. Challenges: Scaling up and local engagement. It enhances forest-based climate mitigation. Secretariat in Washington, D.C.
Partnership for Action on Green Economy (PAGE) 2013 To support countries in transitioning to green economies UN initiative (UNEP, ILO, UNDP); supports 22 countries with policy reforms for low-carbon growth. Achievements: $500M mobilized for green projects. Challenges: Limited scale and funding. It integrates climate into economic planning. Secretariat in Geneva.
Lima Call for Climate Action (COP20) 2014 To prepare for Paris Agreement by mobilizing commitments Adopted at COP20 in Lima, it urged countries to submit INDCs and mobilized $10B for Green Climate Fund. Achievements: 190+ INDCs submitted by 2015. Challenges: Weak ambition in early pledges. It laid groundwork for Paris Agreement. Secretariat in Bonn.
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2015 To achieve sustainable development by 2030 UN 2030 Agenda with 17 goals; SDG13 (climate action) calls for urgent mitigation/adaptation. Achievements: Adopted by 193 countries, shaping national policies (e.g., India’s NAPCC). Challenges: Financing gaps ($4.2T/year) and uneven progress. It integrates climate with development goals. Secretariat in New York.
International Solar Alliance (ISA) 2015 To mobilize solar energy deployment in sun-rich countries India-France initiative with 121 members; aims for $1T in solar investments by 2030. It supports solar projects (e.g., 50 GW in India) and technology transfer. Achievements: 10,000 MW solar projects funded. Challenges: Financing and grid integration. It drives renewable energy globally. Secretariat in Gurugram, India.
Intended Nationally Determined Contributions (INDCs) 2015 To outline national climate pledges before Paris Agreement UNFCCC mechanism; 190+ countries submitted INDCs (e.g., India’s 40% non-fossil energy by 2030). Evolved into NDCs post-Paris. Achievements: Universal participation in pre-Paris pledges. Challenges: Weak initial ambition (3°C+ warming). It formalized national climate commitments. Secretariat in Bonn.
Paris Agreement (COP21) 2015 To limit global warming to well below 2°C, aiming for 1.5°C Adopted at COP21 with 195 parties; mandates NDCs every 5 years, global stocktake, and $100B/year finance for developing countries. Achievements: Universal adoption, 1.5°C goal. Challenges: Insufficient NDCs (2.4°C trajectory), finance delays. It’s the cornerstone of global climate action. Secretariat in Bonn.
Momentum for Change: Climate Neutral Now 2015 To promote climate neutrality by non-state actors UNFCCC initiative; encourages organizations to measure, reduce, and offset emissions. Achievements: 500+ entities (e.g., Microsoft) pledged neutrality. Challenges: Limited uptake in developing nations. It showcases innovative climate solutions. Secretariat in Bonn.
Kigali Amendment to Montreal Protocol 2016 To phase down hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs) Adopted in Kigali with 146 parties; targets HFCs (GHGs with 1,000x CO2 potency). Achievements: Projected to avoid 105 Gt CO2e by 2050. Challenges: High costs for cooling sector transitions. It enhances Montreal Protocol’s climate impact. Secretariat in Nairobi.
Marrakech Partnership (COP22) 2016 To accelerate Paris Agreement implementation through non-state actors Launched at COP22, it engages businesses, cities, and NGOs in climate action. Achievements: 15,000+ non-state commitments (e.g., net-zero pledges). Challenges: Coordination and accountability gaps. It amplifies bottom-up climate efforts. Secretariat in Bonn.
Talanoa Dialogue (COP23) 2017 To enhance climate ambition through inclusive dialogue Fiji-led UNFCCC process at COP23; facilitated stakeholder inputs for NDC updates. Achievements: Informed 2018 Paris Rulebook. Challenges: Limited binding outcomes. It paved the way for global stocktake. Secretariat in Bonn.
Chile-Madrid Time for Action (COP25) 2019 To urge stronger climate ambition and NDC updates Adopted at COP25 in Madrid (relocated from Chile); emphasized pre-2020 action and carbon market rules (Article 6). Achievements: Pushed for enhanced NDCs. Challenges: Unresolved carbon market rules, weak ambition. It set the stage for COP26. Secretariat in Bonn.
Glasgow Climate Pact (COP26) 2021 To strengthen Paris Agreement implementation Adopted at COP26 in Glasgow; calls for phasing down coal, doubling adaptation finance ($40B/year), and annual NDC updates. Launched Global Methane Pledge. Achievements: First explicit coal phase-down, $100B finance goal met. Challenges: Weak fossil fuel language, finance gaps. It advanced global ambition. Secretariat in Bonn.
Global Methane Pledge 2021 To reduce global methane emissions by 30% by 2030 Launched at COP26 with 150+ countries; targets methane from fossil fuels, agriculture, waste (20% of GHG emissions). Achievements: 50 countries with methane plans. Challenges: Monitoring and enforcement gaps. It addresses short-lived climate pollutants for rapid impact. Secretariat in Washington, D.C.
UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration 2021 To prevent, halt, and reverse ecosystem degradation UNEP/FAO initiative (2021–2030); aims to restore 1B hectares globally. Achievements: 100+ countries with restoration projects (e.g., India’s Green India Mission). Challenges: Funding ($100B/year needed) and land conflicts. It supports climate resilience and SDG 15. Secretariat in Nairobi/Rome.
Global Plastic Treaty (INC Process) 2022 To end plastic pollution through a legally binding treaty UNEA resolution (UNEP/EA.5/Res.14); Intergovernmental Negotiating Committee (INC-1 to INC-5) targets lifecycle management of plastics. Achievements: 175 countries engaged, draft by 2024. Challenges: Industry resistance, waste management gaps. Expected entry 2025, it addresses marine pollution (SDG 14). Secretariat in Nairobi.
Loss and Damage Fund 2022 To provide financial support for climate-vulnerable countries Established at COP27 in Sharm El-Sheikh; operationalized at COP28 with $700M+ initial pledges. It funds irreversible climate impacts (e.g., sea-level rise in SIDS). Achievements: First dedicated fund for loss/damage. Challenges: Funding scale ($580B/year needed) and eligibility disputes. It addresses climate justice. Secretariat hosted by World Bank.
Global Stocktake 2023 To assess collective progress under Paris Agreement First stocktake at COP28; found 1.5°C goal at risk, urged tripling renewables (11,000 GW by 2030) and fossil fuel transition. Achievements: Guided NDC updates for 2025. Challenges: Non-binding recommendations. It drives global accountability. Secretariat in Bonn.
UAE Consensus (COP28) 2023 To accelerate climate action post-global stocktake Adopted at COP28 in Dubai; first explicit call for fossil fuel transition, tripling renewables, and doubling energy efficiency by 2030. Achievements: $85B mobilized, loss/damage fund operationalized. Challenges: Weak phase-out language, finance gaps. It sets ambitious targets for COP30. Secretariat in Bonn.
Coalition for Sovereign Debt Conversions for Climate and Conservation 2024 To fund climate and nature through debt-for-nature swaps Led by WWF, Conservation International; unlocks $100B+ by restructuring debt in 20+ countries (e.g., Gabon’s $500M swap). Achievements: 5 pilot projects launched. Challenges: Scaling and creditor coordination. It supports climate adaptation and biodiversity. Secretariat in Gland, Switzerland.
Baku Climate Finance Goal (COP29) 2024 To set a new climate finance target for developing countries Adopted at COP29 in Baku; sets $300B/year goal post-2020, strengthening carbon markets (Article 6). Achievements: Triples previous $100B target. Challenges: Funding delivery and private sector engagement. It addresses Global South demands for equity. Secretariat in Bonn.

Law/Act/Policy Year Description/Key Provisions Related Rules/Guidelines Justification for Disaster Management Relevance
Indian Meteorological Department Act 1875 Establishes the India Meteorological Department (IMD) for weather forecasting and early warnings for cyclones, floods, droughts, heat waves, and cloudbursts; provides real-time alerts critical for disaster preparedness. IMD Guidelines on Weather Forecasting and Early Warning Protocols (updated periodically). Directly supports disaster management by enabling early warnings for natural disasters like cyclones, floods, and heat waves, facilitating timely evacuations and coordinated responses (e.g., Cyclone Amphan, 2020).
Atomic Energy Act, 1962 (Amended 1987) 1962 Regulates nuclear facilities to prevent nuclear disasters; mandates emergency preparedness, radiation safety, and response protocols; post-Fukushima amendments enhanced safety measures. AERB Safety Codes; NDMA Guidelines for Nuclear and Radiological Emergencies (2009). Directly supports disaster management by ensuring preparedness and response for nuclear and radiological emergencies, critical for man-made disaster mitigation.
Public Liability Insurance Act, 1991 1991 Provides immediate relief to victims of chemical and industrial accidents; mandates insurance for industries handling hazardous substances; ensures compensation for disaster-affected communities. Public Liability Insurance Rules, 1991; NDMA Chemical Disaster Compensation Guidelines. Directly supports disaster management by ensuring financial compensation for victims of industrial disasters (e.g., Bhopal 1984), facilitating rapid recovery and rehabilitation.
Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) Notification (under Environment Protection Act) 1991 Regulates coastal development to mitigate cyclone and tsunami impacts; protects mangroves, coral reefs, and coastal ecosystems; restricts construction in high-risk zones. CRZ Notification, 2011; CRZ Rules, 2019; NDMA Coastal Disaster Guidelines. Directly supports disaster management by protecting coastal ecosystems that buffer natural disasters like cyclones and tsunamis (e.g., 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami), aligning with coastal resilience strategies.
Chemical Accidents (Emergency Planning, Preparedness, and Response) Rules 1996 Issued under Environment Protection Act; mandates emergency plans for chemical industries; establishes Central, State, and District Crisis Groups for rapid response to chemical disasters. NDMA Guidelines for Chemical Disasters (2020); State Crisis Group Protocols. Directly supports disaster management by ensuring preparedness and response mechanisms for chemical disasters, critical after incidents like Vizag gas leak (2020).
Disaster Management Act, 2005 2005 Core legislation mandating disaster risk reduction, preparedness, response, and recovery for all disasters; creates National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) and frameworks for national, state, and district-level disaster management. National Disaster Management Rules, 2005; NDMA Guidelines (e.g., Floods, Cyclones, Earthquakes); National Disaster Management Plan, 2016. Cornerstone of disaster management; provides legal and financial frameworks for all natural (e.g., floods, earthquakes) and man-made (e.g., chemical, nuclear) disasters, ensuring coordinated response.
National Building Code, 2005 (Revised 2016) 2005 Provides guidelines for disaster-resilient construction, including seismic, flood, and cyclone-resistant designs; mandatory for public buildings; supports structural safety. Seismic Zone Guidelines; NDMA Earthquake and Flood-Resistant Construction Guidelines. Directly supports disaster management by ensuring buildings withstand natural disasters like earthquakes and floods, reducing collapse risks (e.g., 2001 Gujarat earthquake).
National Policy on Disaster Management 2009 Policy framework under Disaster Management Act; emphasizes proactive risk reduction, community participation, and multi-hazard preparedness for all disasters; guides national and state actions. NDMA Guidelines on Multi-Hazard Preparedness; National Disaster Management Plan, 2016. Directly supports disaster management by providing a strategic vision for risk reduction and preparedness, aligning national efforts for all disasters.
National Disaster Response Fund (NDRF) Rules 2010 Establishes NDRF under Disaster Management Act; provides financial assistance for immediate relief and rehabilitation in major disasters; managed by NDMA and Ministry of Home Affairs. NDRF Allocation Guidelines; SDRF Norms; NDMA Relief Guidelines. Directly supports disaster management by ensuring funding for rapid relief and recovery for all disasters, critical for operations like 2018 Kerala floods.
Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 2025 Amends the 2005 Act to include explicit provisions for climate-induced disasters (e.g., heat waves, glacial lake outbursts); mandates minimum relief standards; enhances penalties for non-compliance. Updated NDMA Guidelines (2025); Revised National Disaster Management Plan (pending 2025). Directly supports disaster management by updating the legal framework to address emerging climate risks and improve accountability for all disasters.

Directly supports disaster management by building human capacity for prevention and response across all disaster types, training over 100,000 officials annually.

Law/Treaty/Framework Year Description/Key Provisions Related Rules/Guidelines Justification for Disaster Management Relevance
Convention on Early Notification of a Nuclear Accident 1986 Adopted post-Chernobyl by IAEA; requires states to notify others of nuclear accidents with transboundary impacts; mandates information sharing for response and mitigation. IAEA Safety Standards; NDMA Guidelines for Nuclear Emergencies (where applicable). Directly supports disaster management by ensuring rapid international notification and coordination for nuclear disasters, reducing transboundary harm (e.g., Chernobyl, 1986).
Convention on Assistance in the Case of a Nuclear Accident or Radiological Emergency 1986 Adopted by IAEA; facilitates international assistance (technical, humanitarian) for nuclear or radiological emergencies; establishes frameworks for mutual aid. IAEA Emergency Response Protocols; IFRC Guidelines on International Disaster Response. Directly supports disaster management by enabling cross-border assistance for nuclear disasters, ensuring timely response to man-made radiological events.
Tampere Convention on the Provision of Telecommunication Resources for Disaster Mitigation and Relief Operations 1998 UN treaty; facilitates provision of telecommunication equipment and personnel for disaster response; reduces regulatory barriers (e.g., customs) for emergency telecom. ITU Emergency Telecommunications Guidelines; UNOCHA Coordination Protocols. Directly supports disaster management by ensuring communication infrastructure for all disasters (natural and man-made), critical for coordination (e.g., 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami).
Hyogo Framework for Action 2005–2015: Building the Resilience of Nations and Communities to Disasters 2005 Non-binding UN framework; outlines five priorities: governance, risk assessment, knowledge, preparedness, and recovery; adopted at UN World Conference on DRR. UNDRR Monitoring Guidelines; Hyogo Framework Progress Reports. Global blueprint for disaster risk reduction; addressed all disasters (natural: floods, earthquakes; man-made: chemical spills), influencing national policies and reducing losses.
Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Agreement on Disaster Management and Emergency Response 2005 Regional treaty; promotes ASEAN cooperation for DRR, preparedness, and response; includes ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance (AHA Centre). AADMER Work Programme 2021–2025; ASEAN Regional Disaster Emergency Response Simulation Exercise (ARDEX). Directly supports disaster management in ASEAN by enhancing regional response to natural (typhoons, earthquakes) and man-made disasters, critical for Southeast Asia’s vulnerability.
African Union Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa (Kampala Convention) 2009 Regional treaty; first binding agreement on internally displaced persons (IDPs); addresses displacement caused by disasters, requiring prevention and assistance. AU Guidelines on IDP Protection; UNDRR Africa Regional Platform. Directly supports disaster management by addressing displacement from natural (floods, droughts) and man-made (chemical accidents) disasters in Africa.
Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 2015 Non-binding UN framework; sets 7 global targets and 4 priorities: understanding risk, governance, resilience investment, and preparedness/recovery; adopted by 187 UN Member States. Sendai Framework Monitor; UNDRR Guidelines for DRR Implementation. Global standard for DRR; covers all disasters (natural: cyclones, earthquakes; man-made: nuclear, biological), integrated with SDGs, reducing global losses.
Draft Articles on the Protection of Persons in the Event of Disasters 2016 (Ongoing, Binding Instrument Targeted by 2027) ILC draft; outlines state duties to protect persons, seek/receive assistance, and reduce disaster risks; endorsed by UNGA Resolution 79/128 (2024) for finalization by 2027. ILC Commentaries; IFRC Guidelines on International Disaster Law. Emerging binding law for all disasters; addresses gaps in response and prevention, emphasizing human rights and state obligations (e.g., for floods, industrial accidents).
European Union Civil Protection Mechanism 2019 (Revised) Regional framework; coordinates EU member states’ disaster response; includes rescEU (reserve capacities for equipment, teams); supports prevention and preparedness. EU Civil Protection Guidelines; rescEU Operational Protocols. Directly supports disaster management in Europe for natural (floods, wildfires) and man-made (chemical spills) disasters, enhancing cross-border response.
